checks.title: No security group in a region with active network interfaces opens SSH (port 22) to 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0

verify.pass_when_text: No inbound rule of a security group in a region with at least one network interface in use (active ENI) opens port 22 to 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0, whether or not the group is attached to an interface: Drata evaluates all security groups in regions with active ENIs. A tcp rule whose port range contains 22 and a rule with protocol -1 (all traffic) count. A security group as the source, a specific CIDR or a prefix list (not expanded) do not count. Security groups in a region with no ENI in use do not apply.

vanta.test: No security group allows unrestricted IPv4 ingress to remote administration ports
No security group allows unrestricted IPv6 ingress (::/0) to remote administration ports

steps: Identify who connects over SSH to security group {resource_id} today (the finding's detail.ip_permissions and the VPC Flow Logs) and first enable an alternative access: Session Manager, or a rule with a fixed CIDR (the office or VPN IP) or with another security group as the source.

Revoke the offending rules with the command: it uses the exact JSON of this finding's detail.ip_permissions (protocol, ports and only the offending CIDRs), so it does not touch any other rule of the group.
Verify with describe-security-groups that no inbound rule open to 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 on the port remains.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
SG_ID="{resource_id}"
# detail.ip_permissions: only this finding's offending rules, with their exact protocol, ports and CIDRs
aws ec2 revoke-security-group-ingress --group-id "$SG_ID" --region "$REGION" --ip-permissions {detail_json:ip_permissions}
remediation.notes: Revoking is immediate and reversible with authorize-security-group-ingress. Risk: cutting off access for whoever connects from the internet today; open the alternative access first. The command uses revoke-security-group-ingress with --ip-permissions {detail_json:ip_permissions}, which is filled in with the exact JSON of the offending rules (stable key detail.ip_permissions: IpProtocol, FromPort, ToPort and only the offending CIDRs): if a rule does not match, AWS answers InvalidPermission.NotFound and touches nothing, and the group's other rules are never revoked. A rule with a range (for example 0-65535) or with protocol -1 also opens other ports: revoking it closes them all, check detail.ip_permissions. Prefix lists are not expanded: if a prefix list contains 0.0.0.0/0, this check does not see it. Drata's article states that a specific CIDR does not count as a pass for test 102: if it keeps failing with specific CIDRs, prefer Session Manager or a security group as the source.

checks.title: No security group in a region with active network interfaces opens HTTP (port 80) to 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0

verify.pass_when_text: No inbound rule of a security group in a region with at least one network interface in use (active ENI) opens port 80 to 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0, whether or not the group is attached to an interface: Drata evaluates all security groups in regions with active ENIs. drata.name: AWS Security Groups HTTP Access Restricted

steps: Decide what to do with port 80 of security group {resource_id}: (a) close it and serve only 443, which is what Drata test 291 asks for, or (b) keep it on an ALB that only redirects to HTTPS.
Option (a): confirm that port 443 is open and that no client depends on plain HTTP, and revoke the offending rules with the command (exact JSON of detail.ip_permissions).
Option (b): leave the rule and exclude the resource in Drata with the justification that the load balancer only redirects HTTP to HTTPS (see TLS-002).
Verify the final state of the inbound rules with describe-security-groups.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
SG_ID="{resource_id}"
# detail.ip_permissions: only this finding's offending rules, with their exact protocol, ports and CIDRs
aws ec2 revoke-security-group-ingress --group-id "$SG_ID" --region "$REGION" --ip-permissions {detail_json:ip_permissions}
remediation.notes: An ALB whose port 80 listener only redirects to HTTPS still fails Drata test 291: the test looks at the security group rule, not the listener action. The two ways out are to expose only 443 (close 80) or to exclude the resource in Drata with a justification. If 80 is closed, whoever types http:// can no longer connect instead of being redirected. Revoking is immediate and reversible with authorize-security-group-ingress. Risk: cutting off access for whoever connects from the internet today; open the alternative access first. The command uses revoke-security-group-ingress with --ip-permissions {detail_json:ip_permissions}, which is filled in with the exact JSON of the offending rules (stable key detail.ip_permissions: IpProtocol, FromPort, ToPort and only the offending CIDRs): if a rule does not match, AWS answers InvalidPermission.NotFound and touches nothing, and the group's other rules are never revoked. A rule with a range (for example 0-65535) or with protocol -1 also opens other ports: revoking it closes them all, check detail.ip_permissions. Prefix lists are not expanded: if a prefix list contains 0.0.0.0/0, this check does not see it.

checks.title: No security group in a region with active network interfaces has an 'all traffic' inbound rule from a CIDR

verify.pass_when_text: No inbound rule of a security group in a region with at least one network interface in use has protocol -1 (all traffic) with a CIDR as the source, whatever the CIDR (according to the article for Drata test 119, a CIDR does not count as a pass), whether or not the group is attached to an interface. A security group as the source passes. Security groups in a region with no ENI in use do not apply.

steps: Decide which ports, protocols and sources security group {resource_id} needs and first open those specific rules with authorize-security-group-ingress, so as not to cut legitimate traffic.
Revoke the 'all traffic' rules from a CIDR with the command: it uses the exact JSON of this finding's detail.ip_permissions, so it does not touch any other rule of the group.
Verify that the group no longer has inbound rules with protocol -1 from a CIDR.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
SG_ID="{resource_id}"
# detail.ip_permissions: only this finding's offending rules, with their exact protocol, ports and CIDRs
aws ec2 revoke-security-group-ingress --group-id "$SG_ID" --region "$REGION" --ip-permissions {detail_json:ip_permissions}
remediation.notes: It is the 'all traffic' rule: revoking it cuts everything that depended on it, so the specific rules must be opened first, for example: aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id <sg> --protocol tcp --port 443 --cidr <range> --region <region>. The command uses --ip-permissions {detail_json:ip_permissions}, which is filled in with the exact JSON of this group's -1 rules with a CIDR (stable key detail.ip_permissions); rules with another protocol or with a security group as the source are not touched, and if a rule does not match AWS answers InvalidPermission.NotFound without touching anything. Revoking is reversible with authorize-security-group-ingress.

checks.title: No network ACL allows inbound from 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 to ports 22 or 3389

verify.pass_when_text: No network ACL has an inbound rule with an allow action from 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 on port 22 or 3389 in tcp, udp or all protocols (-1). A range that contains the port counts, and a tcp or udp entry without a PortRange covers all ports. Rule order is not modeled: like the CIS control, any allow of that kind is reported even if an earlier rule blocks it.

drata.name: AWS Network ACLs Public Remote Server Administration Access Restricted

vanta.test: No network ACL allows unrestricted ingress (0.0.0.0/0) to remote administration ports

steps: See the inbound rules that allow traffic from any source in NACL {resource_id} (first block, read-only) and note the affected rule numbers (detail.entries).

Decide for each rule: if the protocol is -1, split it into tcp and udp without 22 or 3389 plus icmp (second block for IPv4, third for IPv6; they need 6 free rule numbers); restrict an administration tcp or udp rule to a CIDR (fourth block) or delete it (fifth block).
Since NACLs are stateless, check that return traffic (ephemeral tcp and udp, icmp) is still allowed in both directions before applying in production: test first on a staging subnet.
Verify that no inbound allow rule from 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 covers 22 or 3389.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
NACL_ID="{resource_id}"
# read-only: inbound allow rules from any source
aws ec2 describe-network-acls --network-acl-ids "$NACL_ID" --region "$REGION" --query 'NetworkAcls[0].Entries[?Egress==`false` && RuleAction==`allow` && (CidrBlock==`0.0.0.0/0` || Ipv6CidrBlock==`::/0`)].[RuleNumber,Protocol,PortRange.From,PortRange.To,CidrBlock,Ipv6CidrBlock]' --output table

REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
NACL_ID="{resource_id}"
RULE_NUMBER="__FILL_IN_RULE_NUMBER__"
EXTRA_1="__FILL_IN_FREE_NUMBER_1__"
EXTRA_2="__FILL_IN_FREE_NUMBER_2__"
EXTRA_3="__FILL_IN_FREE_NUMBER_3__"
EXTRA_4="__FILL_IN_FREE_NUMBER_4__"
EXTRA_5="__FILL_IN_FREE_NUMBER_5__"
EXTRA_6="__FILL_IN_FREE_NUMBER_6__"
# WARNING: only for the IPv4 rule with protocol -1 (all protocols, rule 100 of the default NACL). NACLs are stateless: if only tcp were left, UDP (DNS replies, NTP) and ICMP of the whole subnet would be cut. That is why tcp and udp without 22 or 3389 (23-3388 and 3390-65535), and ICMP, are created first, with 6 free rule numbers (lower than any deny's); only then is the original rule replaced with tcp 1-21. If one of the creations fails, the original rule is not touched (the chain stops with &&)
aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry --network-acl-id "$NACL_ID" --ingress --rule-number "$EXTRA_1" --protocol tcp --port-range From=23,To=3388 --cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --rule-action allow --region "$REGION" && aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry --network-acl-id "$NACL_ID" --ingress --rule-number "$EXTRA_2" --protocol tcp --port-range From=3390,To=65535 --cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --rule-action allow --region "$REGION" && aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry --network-acl-id "$NACL_ID" --ingress --rule-number "$EXTRA_3" --protocol udp --port-range From=1,To=21 --cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --rule-action allow --region "$REGION" && aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry --network-acl-id "$NACL_ID" --ingress --rule-number "$EXTRA_4" --protocol udp --port-range From=23,To=3388 --cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --rule-action allow --region "$REGION" && aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry --network-acl-id "$NACL_ID" --ingress --rule-number "$EXTRA_5" --protocol udp --port-range From=3390,To=65535 --cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --rule-action allow --region "$REGION" && aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry --network-acl-id "$NACL_ID" --ingress --rule-number "$EXTRA_6" --protocol 1 --icmp-type-code Type=-1,Code=-1 --cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --rule-action allow --region "$REGION" && aws ec2 replace-network-acl-entry --network-acl-id "$NACL_ID" --ingress --rule-number "$RULE_NUMBER" --protocol tcp --port-range From=1,To=21 --cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --rule-action allow --region "$REGION"

REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
NACL_ID="{resource_id}"
RULE_NUMBER="__FILL_IN_RULE_NUMBER__"
EXTRA_1="__FILL_IN_FREE_NUMBER_1__"
EXTRA_2="__FILL_IN_FREE_NUMBER_2__"
EXTRA_3="__FILL_IN_FREE_NUMBER_3__"
EXTRA_4="__FILL_IN_FREE_NUMBER_4__"
EXTRA_5="__FILL_IN_FREE_NUMBER_5__"
EXTRA_6="__FILL_IN_FREE_NUMBER_6__"
# WARNING: only for the IPv6 rule with protocol -1 (all protocols, rule 100 of the default NACL). NACLs are stateless: if only tcp were left, UDP (DNS replies, NTP) and ICMP of the whole subnet would be cut. That is why tcp and udp without 22 or 3389 (23-3388 and 3390-65535), and ICMP, are created first, with 6 free rule numbers (lower than any deny's); only then is the original rule replaced with tcp 1-21. If one of the creations fails, the original rule is not touched (the chain stops with &&)
aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry --network-acl-id "$NACL_ID" --ingress --rule-number "$EXTRA_1" --protocol tcp --port-range From=23,To=3388 --ipv6-cidr-block ::/0 --rule-action allow --region "$REGION" && aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry --network-acl-id "$NACL_ID" --ingress --rule-number "$EXTRA_2" --protocol tcp --port-range From=3390,To=65535 --ipv6-cidr-block ::/0 --rule-action allow --region "$REGION" && aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry --network-acl-id "$NACL_ID" --ingress --rule-number "$EXTRA_3" --protocol udp --port-range From=1,To=21 --ipv6-cidr-block ::/0 --rule-action allow --region "$REGION" && aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry --network-acl-id "$NACL_ID" --ingress --rule-number "$EXTRA_4" --protocol udp --port-range From=23,To=3388 --ipv6-cidr-block ::/0 --rule-action allow --region "$REGION" && aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry --network-acl-id "$NACL_ID" --ingress --rule-number "$EXTRA_5" --protocol udp --port-range From=3390,To=65535 --ipv6-cidr-block ::/0 --rule-action allow --region "$REGION" && aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry --network-acl-id "$NACL_ID" --ingress --rule-number "$EXTRA_6" --protocol 58 --icmp-type-code Type=-1,Code=-1 --ipv6-cidr-block ::/0 --rule-action allow --region "$REGION" && aws ec2 replace-network-acl-entry --network-acl-id "$NACL_ID" --ingress --rule-number "$RULE_NUMBER" --protocol tcp --port-range From=1,To=21 --ipv6-cidr-block ::/0 --rule-action allow --region "$REGION"

REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
NACL_ID="{resource_id}"
RULE_NUMBER="__FILL_IN_RULE_NUMBER__"
PROTOCOL="__FILL_IN_PROTOCOL_TCP_OR_UDP__"
PORT_FROM="__FILL_IN_PORT_FROM__"
PORT_TO="__FILL_IN_PORT_TO__"
ADMIN_CIDR="__FILL_IN_ADMIN_CIDR__"
# only for an administration tcp or udp rule (a rule with protocol -1 does not accept --port-range: use the split block); for IPv6 use --ipv6-cidr-block
aws ec2 replace-network-acl-entry --network-acl-id "$NACL_ID" --ingress --rule-number "$RULE_NUMBER" --protocol "$PROTOCOL" --port-range From="$PORT_FROM",To="$PORT_TO" --cidr-block "$ADMIN_CIDR" --rule-action allow --region "$REGION"

REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
NACL_ID="{resource_id}"
RULE_NUMBER="__FILL_IN_RULE_NUMBER__"
aws ec2 delete-network-acl-entry --network-acl-id "$NACL_ID" --ingress --rule-number "$RULE_NUMBER" --region "$REGION"
remediation.notes: WARNING: changing the rules of a NACL can cut the traffic of the entire subnet (DNS, NTP, replies to outbound connections) even if the command succeeds. Each VPC's default NACL comes with rule 100 that allows all inbound traffic from 0.0.0.0/0, so Drata 227 and CIS report it in every account. The split blocks replace that protocol -1 rule with tcp and udp on 1-21, 23-3388 and 3390-65535 plus icmp (icmpv6 on IPv6), so that ephemeral return traffic stays allowed; only 22 and 3389 are closed (return traffic with destination port 22 or 3389 is rare, but check it if it is used). The alternative is to associate the subnets with a NACL of their own. A typical ephemeral range (1024-65535) contains 3389 and is also reported: split it into 1024-3388 and 3390-65535. NACLs are stateless and are evaluated by rule number: the free numbers must be lower than those of any deny rules in the NACL. Outbound rules are not touched. Apply first on a staging subnet and check DNS and outbound connections. The split blocks only recreate tcp, udp and icmp: the other protocols that the protocol -1 rule covered (ESP and AH of a site-to-site VPN or IPsec, GRE, tunnel protocols) lose their permission when it is replaced; if the subnet uses them, add an allow rule for each one (with another free number) before replacing the original rule.

checks.title: The default security group of each VPC has no inbound or outbound rules

verify.pass_when_text: The default security group of each VPC, in all enabled regions, has no inbound or outbound rules (the one AWS creates comes with an outbound rule that allows everything). It is a per-VPC test, like Drata's 233 and Vanta's 35.

drata.name: AWS VPC Default Security Groups Restrict All Traffic

vanta.test: The default security group in every VPC blocks all traffic

steps: Check which network interfaces use the default security group of VPC {resource_id} today (first block, read-only): when it is emptied they lose the traffic that depended on its rules.
Move those resources, if there are any, to a security group of their own with the minimum rules.

Revoke the inbound and outbound rules of the default group (second and third block): the blocks stop with a message if any network interface uses the group; if there is none, they revoke only the rules the group has at that moment.
Verify that the default group has no rules any more.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
VPC_ID="{resource_id}"
SG_ID=$(aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters "Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC_ID" "Name=group-name,Values=default" --region "$REGION" --query 'SecurityGroups[0].GroupId' --output text)
# read-only: network interfaces that use the default security group
aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces --filters "Name=group-id,Values=$SG_ID" --region "$REGION" --query 'NetworkInterfaces[].[NetworkInterfaceId,Description,Status]' --output table

REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
VPC_ID="{resource_id}"
SG_ID=$(aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters "Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC_ID" "Name=group-name,Values=default" --region "$REGION" --query 'SecurityGroups[0].GroupId' --output text)
ENIS=$(aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces --filters "Name=group-id,Values=$SG_ID" --region "$REGION" --query 'length(NetworkInterfaces)' --output text)
RULES=$(aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids "$SG_ID" --region "$REGION" --query 'SecurityGroups[0].IpPermissions' --output json)
# stops if there are network interfaces using the group (or if they could not be counted): emptying it would cut their traffic
if [ -z "$SG_ID" ] || [ "$SG_ID" = "None" ]; then echo "STOPPED: the default security group was not found"; elif [ "$ENIS" != "0" ]; then echo "STOPPED: there are network interfaces that use the default security group (or they could not be counted); move them to another group before emptying it:"; aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces --filters "Name=group-id,Values=$SG_ID" --region "$REGION" --query 'NetworkInterfaces[].[NetworkInterfaceId,Description,Status]' --output table; elif [ -n "$RULES" ] && [ "$RULES" != "[]" ]; then aws ec2 revoke-security-group-ingress --group-id "$SG_ID" --region "$REGION" --ip-permissions "$RULES"; fi

REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
VPC_ID="{resource_id}"
SG_ID=$(aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters "Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC_ID" "Name=group-name,Values=default" --region "$REGION" --query 'SecurityGroups[0].GroupId' --output text)
ENIS=$(aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces --filters "Name=group-id,Values=$SG_ID" --region "$REGION" --query 'length(NetworkInterfaces)' --output text)
RULES=$(aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids "$SG_ID" --region "$REGION" --query 'SecurityGroups[0].IpPermissionsEgress' --output json)
# stops if there are network interfaces using the group (or if they could not be counted): emptying it would cut their traffic
if [ -z "$SG_ID" ] || [ "$SG_ID" = "None" ]; then echo "STOPPED: the default security group was not found"; elif [ "$ENIS" != "0" ]; then echo "STOPPED: there are network interfaces that use the default security group (or they could not be counted); move them to another group before emptying it:"; aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces --filters "Name=group-id,Values=$SG_ID" --region "$REGION" --query 'NetworkInterfaces[].[NetworkInterfaceId,Description,Status]' --output table; elif [ -n "$RULES" ] && [ "$RULES" != "[]" ]; then aws ec2 revoke-security-group-egress --group-id "$SG_ID" --region "$REGION" --ip-permissions "$RULES"; fi
remediation.notes: A new VPC comes with its default security group with an inbound rule from itself and an outbound rule to everything: both tests (Drata 233, Vanta 35) report it in every account. The default group cannot be deleted. Any resource launched without specifying a security group uses it (RDS, Lambda in a VPC, ECS tasks, console-launched EC2): emptying it with attached resources leaves them without traffic. That is why the first block lists the interfaces that use it and blocks 2 and 3 count those interfaces (describe-network-interfaces with the group-id filter) and, if there are any or they could not be counted, stop with a message without revoking anything: first move those resources to a security group of their own. The commands read the group's current rules and revoke them as they are, without touching any other group. It is reversible by recreating the rules.

checks.title: RDS instances are not public and are not in subnets with a route to an internet gateway

verify.pass_when_text: The instance has PubliclyAccessible=false and none of the subnets in its DB subnet group has an active route to an internet gateway (igw-) for 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0. Each subnet's route table is the explicitly associated one or, if it has none, its VPC's main one. According to Drata test 220, an instance in a public subnet fails even if PubliclyAccessible is false.

vanta.test: RDS instances are not publicly accessible

steps: Confirm who connects to database {resource_id} from outside the VPC and give them another path (VPN, bastion, Session Manager with port forwarding or a proxy inside the VPC): after the change the database is not reachable from the internet.
Turn off PubliclyAccessible on the instance (first block).

If the database is in subnets with a route to an internet gateway (detail.public_subnets), create a DB subnet group with private subnets of the same VPC and move the database to it (second block), in an agreed window.
Verify PubliclyAccessible=false and that the database's subnets no longer have a route to an igw-.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
DB_ID="{resource_id}"
aws rds modify-db-instance --db-instance-identifier "$DB_ID" --no-publicly-accessible --apply-immediately --region "$REGION"

REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
DB_ID="{resource_id}"
SUBNET_GROUP="__FILL_IN_PRIVATE_SUBNET_GROUP_NAME__"
SUBNET_A="__FILL_IN_PRIVATE_SUBNET_AZ_A__"
SUBNET_B="__FILL_IN_PRIVATE_SUBNET_AZ_B__"
aws rds create-db-subnet-group --db-subnet-group-name "$SUBNET_GROUP" --db-subnet-group-description "Subnets privadas" --subnet-ids "$SUBNET_A" "$SUBNET_B" --region "$REGION" && aws rds modify-db-instance --db-instance-identifier "$DB_ID" --db-subnet-group-name "$SUBNET_GROUP" --apply-immediately --region "$REGION"
remediation.notes: There is downtime: changing the DB subnet group moves the instance to another zone and can reboot it (in Multi-AZ, a failover); do it in an agreed window. Whoever uses the public endpoint today can no longer connect, and the DNS endpoint may resolve to another private IP. The database's security group must allow traffic from the new access network. The private subnets must be in the same VPC and cover at least 2 zones. For an Aurora instance, the subnet group is changed on the cluster (modify-db-cluster). A subnet that is 'public' by route even though PubliclyAccessible is false still fails Drata test 220: the only fix is to move it. --apply-immediately also applies any other pending change on the instance.

checks.title: Public ALBs, API Gateway REST APIs and CloudFront distributions have a WAF web ACL associated

verify.pass_when_text: Each internet-facing ALB, each non-private REST API (with all its stages) and each enabled CloudFront distribution has a WAFv2 web ACL associated; there is one row per resource. Internal ALBs, NLBs, private APIs, APIs with no deployed stages and disabled distributions do not apply. HTTP APIs (apigatewayv2) are not evaluated because WAF cannot be associated with them. CLOUDFRONT-scope web ACLs are read in us-east-1 only to suggest an existing one in the finding (detail.available_web_acls).

steps: Decide the web ACL: reuse an existing one in the region or create one with AWS managed rules (AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet), starting in Count mode to observe before blocking.
Create the regional web ACL (first block) and associate it with the ALB (second block) or with each stage of the REST API (third block, one per stage in detail.stages; resource_id is the API ID).
For a CloudFront distribution, create a web ACL with scope CLOUDFRONT in us-east-1 and associate it from the console (Distribution, Security, Web ACL).
Verify that the web ACL exists and that the resource appears as associated (list-resources-for-web-acl).
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
ACL_NAME="__FILL_IN_WEB_ACL_NAME__"
# starts in Count (only counts, does not block) to observe the traffic before blocking; prints the web ACL's ARN
aws wafv2 create-web-acl --name "$ACL_NAME" --scope REGIONAL --default-action Allow={} --visibility-config SampledRequestsEnabled=true,CloudWatchMetricsEnabled=true,MetricName="$ACL_NAME" --rules '[{"Name":"AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet","Priority":0,"Statement":{"ManagedRuleGroupStatement":{"VendorName":"AWS","Name":"AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet"}},"OverrideAction":{"Count":{}},"VisibilityConfig":{"SampledRequestsEnabled":true,"CloudWatchMetricsEnabled":true,"MetricName":"common-rule-set"}}]' --region "$REGION" --query 'Summary.ARN' --output text

REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
ACL_ARN="__FILL_IN_WEB_ACL_ARN__"
LB_ARN=$(aws elbv2 describe-load-balancers --names "{resource_id}" --region "$REGION" --query 'LoadBalancers[0].LoadBalancerArn' --output text) && aws wafv2 associate-web-acl --web-acl-arn "$ACL_ARN" --resource-arn "$LB_ARN" --region "$REGION"

REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
ACL_ARN="__FILL_IN_WEB_ACL_ARN__"
STAGE="__FILL_IN_STAGE__"
# only for a REST API (resource_id is the API ID): repeat for each stage in detail.stages
aws wafv2 associate-web-acl --web-acl-arn "$ACL_ARN" --resource-arn "arn:aws:apigateway:$REGION::/restapis/{resource_id}/stages/$STAGE" --region "$REGION"
remediation.notes: Drata test 122 only requires the web ACL to be associated, but with the rule in Count it does not protect: switch the rules that produce no false positives to Block after reviewing the logs. Cost: WAF charges per web ACL, per rule and per million requests. A regional web ACL serves the ALBs and API Gateways of its region; CloudFront needs one of its own with scope CLOUDFRONT in us-east-1. A CloudFront distribution (resource_id is its ID) is associated with update-distribution (the entire configuration must be resent with its ETag), which is why it is safer to do it from the console; detail.available_web_acls lists the CLOUDFRONT-scope web ACLs that already exist. Enabling the web ACL's logging is a separate check.
